real user can accomplish a job.\n\n## Test Contract\n\nEach test needs a mission card:\n\n- **Running app:** URL, route, or entry point.\n- **User role:** who the agent is pretending to be.\n- **Mission:** the job to accomplish in user language.\n- **Allowed interface:** browser, app UI, keyboard, pointer, accessibility tree, or other user-level controls.\n- **Forbidden shortcuts:** no source inspection, no backend logs, no database queries, no implementation knowledge unless the user explicitly allows it.\n- **Expected completion proof:** the visible state that proves the job is complete.\n- **Failure conditions:** places where \"no error\" still counts as failure.\n\nExample:\n\n```text\nRunning app: http://localhost:3050/session/<id>\nUser role: operator returning to a direct-control session\nMission: determine whether the CLI is waiting for input and clear the unread state by reading it\nAllowed interface: browser UI only\nExpected completion proof: unread state appears until read; after reading, there is no spinner and no unread dot\nFailure conditions: spinner keeps spinning, no visible status changes, user cannot tell what to do, or the app silently does nothing\n```\n\n## How To Run\n\nUse the current harness's browser or UI-control tools. Behave like a user:\n\n1. Open the app at the provided entry point.\n2. Inspect only what a user could perceive.\n3. Decide where to click or type from the interface itself.\n4. Attempt the mission.\n5. Record visible evidence of success or the exact point of failure.\n\nDo not treat clean logs, HTTP 200 responses, or lack of console errors as success. Those are supporting signals only.\n\n## Pass Criteria\n\nThe journey passes only when:\n\n- the agent can understand what to do from the UI,\n- the agent can complete the mission through user-level actions,\n- the visible app state matches the expected completion proof,\n- no stale loading, misleading status, silent no-op, or hidden failure remains.\n\n## Failure Means Work Remains\n\nIf the journey fails, fix the product or the supporting state model. Do not dismiss the failure as \"just the test agent being confused\" unless there is clear evidence the mission was malformed.\n\nCommon product failures:\n\n- the app is technically idle but still shows running state,\n- a click succeeds internally but nothing visible changes,\n- the user cannot discover the next action,\n- the UI hides the real error,\n- the completion state is ambiguous.\n\n## Relationship To Other Tests\n\nAgentic journey tests complement deterministic tests. They do not replace:\n\n- unit tests,\n- integration tests,\n- state-machine tests,\n- accessibility checks,\n- deterministic Playwright assertions.\n\nWhen a journey fails, add deterministic regression coverage for the underlying behavior whenever practical.\n"

Native profiles therefore skipped direct login when a saved password matched the submitted value, even if their bearer credential was missing, expired, or revoked. The same-origin browser profile returned from the authorization function without using the submitted password at all. Fixing that button exposed a second path with the same mistaken model: startup loaded the saved password but never exchanged it for a server-authoritative cookie session. Profile persistence and authentication state had been conflated in both entry points. Separately, the production runner reads and retains `dist/interface/index.html` at startup, so rebuilding the interface without restarting the runner leaves the public domain serving the old hashed JavaScript bundle.\ndocs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-01-connect-must-attempt-authentication.md:7:**Fix:** The current same-origin profile now submits the password through its runtime login endpoint and retries its connection when Connect is pressed. On startup, an unauthenticated same-origin profile with a saved password makes one login attempt, reloads bootstrap to prove the server accepted it, and then connects normally. A rejected password stops at `needs-reauth` without an automatic retry loop. Native profile edits authorize whenever Connect is submitted with a password, regardless of whether the saved password text changed. After rebuilding, the existing production runner was restarted through the restart controller so it loaded the new interface manifest.\ndocs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-01-connect-must-attempt-authentication.md:8:**Verification:** Both focused regression tests were observed failing before their respective fixes and passing afterward. `pnpm vitest run tests/interface/runners/runner-connection.test.ts tests/ui/sidebar-layout.test.ts` passed 56 tests, TypeScript passed, changed-file lint passed, and the web interface built. The targeted Playwright journey `automatically unlocks the current server with its saved password after reload` passed against two temporary real runners after clearing the browser cookie and reloading. After the production restart, the public domain and local build both referenced `main-DWX2wW4Q.js`, and their SHA-256 hashes matched exactly (`c08dcaf7094335ae85afa8956be76af74d851928f88b978a699b2b4f39f5a857`).\ndocs/superpowers/learnings/2026-08-01-connect-must-attempt-authentication.md:9:**Prevention:** Treat Connect as an explicit authentication attempt, and treat reload as a separate return journey that must restore server-authoritative authentication from saved credentials. Decide whether to authenticate from connection and credential state plus the user's action, never from a comparison of secret text. Regression coverage must test every authentication entry point, assert that the password reaches a real login path, clear the server session, revisit the app, and verify that startup restores it without manual UI actions. For live interface changes, rebuild and restart the production runner, then compare the public asset name and hash to the local build before reporting the fix as live.\ndocs/superpowers/learnings/2026-05-24-persisted-reload-zombie-workers.md:7:**Fix:** Added a persisted-bootstrap reconciliation pass for selected runs. Decide whether to authenticate from connection and credential state plus the user's action, never from a comparison of secret text. Regression coverage must test every authentication entry point, assert that the password reaches a real login path, clear the server session, revisit the app, and verify that startup restores it without manual UI actions. <!-- codex-event:{"kind":"progress","timestamp":"2026-08-03T12:15:40.032Z","phase":"commentary"} -->
## Codex progress · 2026-08-03T12:15:40.032Z

I found the exact culprit.

At 10:32 the production runner restarted and loaded the then-current HTML. At 10:36 an agent working on the new “Restart server” button ran the full test suite. One test—`tests/interface/vite-build.test.ts`—runs a real frontend build directly into the same `dist/interface` directory used by the live server. At 10:38:54 it deleted the old hashed JavaScript and wrote a new one, but the already-running server kept the old HTML filename in memory.

So:

- Your already-open app kept working because its JavaScript was already loaded.
- A later fresh PWA launch received the old filename from the server.
- That file had just been deleted by the test build, so it returned 404 and produced a blank screen.
- Clearing data forced another fresh load and therefore could only reproduce it.

That is a test-isolation bug on this machine, not a phone, PWA, or Cloudflare problem. I’m fixing the test now so running the suite cannot overwrite the live frontend again. I’m using the test-first guide because the prevention needs proof that the live build directory stays untouched.

The public server is healthy and answering bootstrap/session requests. The generic wording means the browser didn’t receive a normal structured error such as “incorrect password”; it saw either a network-level failure or had no usable connection object. ## Codex progress · 2026-08-03T12:20:09.371Z

I found your mobile request in the audit log: Android reached the server at 14:14:39 and the password was accepted. The failure happened immediately afterward in the frontend.

The race is in the Connect flow: it tries to reuse a connection object’s API before that connection has finished creating it. On a fast desktop test it’s ready; on a cold mobile PWA after clearing data it often isn’t, so the UI throws the exact generic error you saw even though login succeeded.

I’m moving password authentication into the connection manager so Connect can safely authenticate while the connection is still starting, then retry cleanly. This also keeps the state transition in one place instead of depending on component timing.

Use/customize the shadcn control before hand-building a one-off control.\n- When a scrollable or clipped container holds focusable controls, reserve inner space at least as wide as their outer focus ring or draw the ring inset. Padding outside the clipping viewport does not protect descendant focus rings.\n\n## State And Data\n\n- Always centralize React app state in global single-source-of-truth Manager classes.\n- Components, hooks, and listeners subscribe to Manager updates and use Manager methods to update data.\n- Centralized state does not mean broad subscriptions. Components must subscribe to the smallest slice they need, preferably with selector hooks and equality checks, so unrelated UI does not re-render.\n- Never let app shells, page roots, sidebars, timelines, or other broad containers subscribe to an entire high-churn Manager snapshot when they only need stable fields. Draft text, cursors, hover/open state, search text, and other per-keystroke or per-pointer state need narrow component-level subscriptions.\n- If typing in an input, moving a cursor, toggling a hover/open flag, or editing a small draft makes the whole app repaint, the subscription boundary is wrong even if the data source is centralized.\n- Always implement a custom data manager for any app data structure.\n- Never use separate state variables or arrays as the source of truth.\n- Never send data around in transactions. Pass intent, ids, commands, or Manager method calls instead.\n\n## React Control Flow\n\n- Avoid using `useEffect()` to update state. Prefer `useCallback()` handlers or Manager methods for explicit state transitions.\n- Work ahead of time to avoid callback hell, race conditions, and infinite loops.\n- When debugging React and a fix does not work, explicitly consider whether the root cause is a race condition. Race conditions are common in React.\n- Every async callback, mutation result, timer, poll, or stream message that can update visible state must prove it still owns the current context before mutating Managers or navigation.\n- Use `RefObject` instead of `MutableRefObject`.\n\n## Routing And Modules\n\n- Prefer explicit routing over file-based routing when the framework does not strongly default to file-based routes. Framework-native file routing, such as Next.js App Router, is fine.\n- Never use `require()` to import modules. Use `import` instead.\n- Avoid `npm` by default. Use `pnpm` for package installation, scripts, and lockfiles unless the user or existing project explicitly chooses another package manager.\n\n## Next.js And SSR Defaults\n\n- Treat `\"use client\"` as a boundary with a cost. Do not put an entire page, app shell, sidebar, timeline, composer, settings surface, and data boot path behind one giant client component unless there is a deliberate reason.\n- SSR is only useful if the initial HTML contains meaningful above-the-fold UI or data. If `curl` for the route only shows a boot shell, script payloads, or empty placeholders, the route is not meaningfully server-rendered even if SSR is technically enabled.\n- Server-render the first useful screen by fetching route-stable bootstrap data on the server: auth/session state, settings needed to choose the shell, selected route ids, and initial page/snapshot data. Hydrate Managers or query caches from that bootstrap data; do not wait for client `useEffect()` plus client fetches before the first meaningful paint.\n- Use client effects for browser-only concerns: localStorage-only preferences, notifications, SSE/WebSocket subscriptions, focus management, and post-paint refreshes. Do not use effects as the only path for data required to decide what the initial screen is.\n- In Next dev, first request time includes compilation. Distinguish cold compile cost from runtime slowness before optimizing the wrong layer.\n\n## Import And Bundle Hygiene\n\n- Keep imports proportional to the UI being rendered. Do not import an entire complex surface for a tiny control; split shared tiny controls into their own files instead of importing them from heavy feature modules.\n- Lazy-load rarely opened or route-conditional surfaces with dynamic imports: settings dialogs, side panels, file viewers, terminals, worker inspectors, onboarding flows, QR/pairing dialogs, and large markdown/code viewers.\n- Avoid package and barrel imports that drag in whole icon packs, design systems, syntax highlighters, markdown stacks, charting libraries, or component suites for one glyph or one primitive. Inline small SVG paths or use local assets when that is cheaper and stable.\n- Prefer native browser controls for small, ordinary selects and pickers. Do not import a popover/dialog/menu stack for a low-value dropdown unless search, virtualization, or rich item rendering is genuinely needed.\n- Use subpath imports when a package supports them. Avoid root package imports from large UI libraries if a narrower entrypoint exists.\n- After dependency or UI-shell changes, inspect the emitted dev chunks or traces. Verify whether heavy modules moved out of the root chunk rather than assuming dynamic import worked.\n\n## Performance Debugging\n\n- Start with evidence: dev server logs, route timings, emitted chunk sizes, module counts, and initial HTML content.\n- Separate long-lived requests from slow requests. SSE, streaming, and hanging fetches can show huge durations in logs without blocking page paint.\n- Check recent dependency additions first when compile time suddenly explodes. A single icon, markdown, chart, or UI package can add thousands of modules.\n- For Next.js root-load complaints, answer three questions before changing code: what compiled, what HTML was returned, and what client-side requests gated the first useful paint?\n\n## Frontend Configuration\n\n- Never store frontend string literals or UI settings in `.env` files.\n- Put frontend strings and settings in normal source files, inline arrays, or `.json` files so they remain reviewable, testable, and versioned with the UI.\n\n## Internationalization\n\n- For meaningful React UI work, offer language support as an option when the user has not already decided: \"Should we support other languages? If yes, I will wire user-facing copy through i18n resources now instead of hardcoding strings.\"\n- If the user says yes, asks for translation/i18n/language/locale support, or reports that language switching only updates part of the UI, use `implementing-react-i18n`.\n- Use the i18n library's `t(\"key\", params?)` function for every user-facing string. Use `useI18nSnapshot()` only to subscribe React components so language changes repaint.\n- Never name variables with locale codes or locale-like names such as `it`, `en`, `enUS`, `locIt`, or `locEnUs`.\n\n## Settings UI\n\n- For settings dialogs, preferences panels, configuration modals, option tabs, or UI settings surfaces, use `designing-settings-dialogs`.\n---\nname: client-server-state-invariants\ndescription: Use when planning, building, reviewing, or debugging React apps with server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, background jobs, persistence, or client/server synchronization\n---\n\n# Client Server State Invariants\n\nReact bugs often expose deeper ownership mistakes. When client state, server state, cache state, stream state, and persisted state all exist, every plan needs explicit invariants.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nNo UI surface may treat data as authoritative unless the payload proves ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and terminal state.\n\nIf those words are missing from the plan, the plan is probably baking in a race condition.\n\n## Planning Checklist\n\nFor every React app that reads server/runtime state, the plan must answer:\n\n1. **Owner:** What owns this state: server, client manager, URL, cache, stream, local storage, or worker/runtime?\n2. **Token:** What owner token protects async results: `requestId`, `runId`, `projectPath`, `operationId`, `workerId + seq`, or equivalent?\n3. **Provenance:** Is data server-authoritative, optimistic, cached preview, partial update, or historical fallback?\n4. **Completeness:** Does the payload declare what scope it is complete for? What may it erase?\n5. **Ordering:** What stable order is used: monotonic seq, `(createdAt, id)`, version, or cursor?\n6. **State machine:** What are the legal states, terminal states, and transitions?\n7. **Events:** Which server decisions are named events rather than client-side derivations?\n8. **Loading shape:** Which states are bootstrap, first load, incremental refresh, reconnect, resync, recovery, and terminal error?\n9. **Fallbacks:** Which legacy/fallback rows can render, and only after what authority is loaded?\n10. **Tests:** Which race, stale-response, event-sequence, reconnect, and merge tests prove the invariants?\n\n## Invariants To Require\n\n- Cached and optimistic data may pre-render, but cannot satisfy full-load gates.\n- Partial snapshots may add or refine state, but may not erase optimistic objects, delivered user input, read markers, or stream entries unless they declare complete scope.\n- Every async response checks that its owner token still matches before mutating visible state.\n- Mutation success handlers may navigate or clear UI only if they still own the current context, unless the action explicitly creates a new selected context.\n- Timers and polling callbacks re-check ownership immediately before acting.\n- Server decisions are emitted as named events; the client does not infer decisions by diffing snapshots.\n- SSE/WebSocket streams have event ids, replay/resume, and an explicit resync path.\n- Loading booleans are split by lifecycle stage. A leaf stream refresh must not unmount the whole page.\n- Append-only content has one writer, one reader, stable ids, and monotonic cursors.\n- Fallback DB rows or historical rows are gated behind stream loading and deduped by stable id plus safe equivalence.\n- Status classifiers distinguish active, runnable, blocked, awaiting user, terminal, stale, and recoverable states.\n- \"Latest\" queries have deterministic tie-breakers. Timestamp-only ordering is not enough.\n- Hot paths use bounded reads and do not synchronously load large bodies, bridge probes, schema setup, or heavy app graphs.\n- Process-local caches have explicit TTL/size bounds and invalidation rules.\n\n## Test Matrix\n\nPick the rows that match the work. Do not rely on one happy-path UI test.\n\n| Risk | Test shape |\n| --- | --- |\n| Stale async response | Start request A, switch owner, resolve A, assert it cannot mutate B |\n| Optimistic object erased | Create local optimistic state, apply stale/partial snapshot, assert object remains |\n| Cache masquerades as loaded | Hydrate cache preview, assert full-load gate waits for server authority |\n| Mutation steals navigation | Start mutation, switch selection, resolve mutation, assert focus stays put |\n| Timer/poll stale-fire | Use fake timers or deferred promises; callback must re-check owner before acting |\n| Snapshot merge erases stream | Apply partial snapshot missing known entries, assert entries/read markers remain |\n| Event stream gap | Bootstrap snapshot, emit events during disconnect, reconnect with last id, assert replay or resync |\n| Server decision invisible | Exercise branch and assert named event such as `blocked`, `refused`, `gave_up`, or `error.surfaced` |\n| State classifier wrong | Table-test every status into active/runnable/terminal/recoverable buckets |\n| Fallback duplicates stream | Load fallback rows then stream entries, assert no duplicate or false chronology |\n| Hot path bloats | Assert snapshots carry cursors not bodies; route returns before DB/heavy imports when possible |\n| Timestamp tie | Insert equal timestamps, assert deterministic order by id/seq |\n\nUse headless HTTP/SSE tests for control-plane decisions. Use React/unit tests for manager merging and ownership guards. Use Playwright only for real UI layout, focus, scroll, mobile computed styles, and visible affordances.\n\n## Refuse These Shapes\n\n- one `isLoading` boolean for bootstrap, refresh, reconnect, and recovery;\n- cache or optimistic data treated as authoritative without provenance;\n- async callbacks that mutate state without checking owner tokens;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- snapshot diffs used as the only way to know what happened;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- timestamp-only \"latest\" queries;\n- parallel transcript or persistence surfaces that the frontend must reconcile;\n- unbounded process caches introduced to hide slow storage;\n- tests that prove only the DOM result when the bug is a server decision.\n\n## Review Prompt\n\nAsk this before ## Codex progress · 2026-08-03T12:21:36.861Z

The regression test now proves the cold-start race and passes with the fix: Connect can authenticate before the connection’s API is attached, and the manager then reconnects to an online state.

I’m checking the frontend types and lint now. After that I’ll rebuild and restart the existing runner in one sequence so the fixed mobile code is actually served; active worker turns may briefly reconnect, but conversations and history remain intact.

## Codex progress · 2026-08-03T12:22:58.083Z

I found the exact failure: the server accepted the mobile password, but the app tried to use its connection object before that object had finished starting. I’ve moved login into the connection manager so it can safely wait for startup; I’m updating the affected test now, then I’ll rebuild and restart the live tunnel server.

[
  {

  {
    "type": "input_text",
    "text": "# Connect Must Attempt Authentication\n\n**Date:** 2026-08-01\n**Context:** OmniHarness server profiles, saved passwords, and browser/native authorization\n**Symptom:** Entering the server password in Edit server and pressing Connect initially closed the dialog but left the interface on the password screen. After that action was fixed, it worked only when repeated manually; clearing or losing the browser session and reloading still showed the password screen even though the profile retained the password.\n**Root Cause:** The edit flow treated an unchanged saved password as evidence that authorization did not need to run. Native profiles therefore skipped direct login when a saved password matched the submitted value, even if their bearer credential was missing, expired, or revoked. The same-origin browser profile returned from the authorization function without using the submitted password at all. Fixing that button exposed a second path with the same mistaken model: startup loaded the saved password but never exchanged it for a server-authoritative cookie session. Profile persistence and authentication state had been conflated in both entry points. Separately, the production runner reads and retains `dist/interface/index.html` at startup, so rebuilding the interface without restarting the runner leaves the public domain serving the old hashed JavaScript bundle.\n**Fix:** The current same-origin profile now submits the password through its runtime login endpoint and retries its connection when Connect is pressed. On startup, an unauthenticated same-origin profile with a saved password makes one login attempt, reloads bootstrap to prove the server accepted it, and then connects normally. A rejected password stops at `needs-reauth` without an automatic retry loop. Native profile edits authorize whenever Connect is submitted with a password, regardless of whether the saved password text changed. After rebuilding, the existing production runner was restarted through the restart controller so it loaded the new interface manifest.\n**Verification:** Both focused regression tests were observed failing before their respective fixes and passing afterward. `pnpm vitest run tests/interface/runners/runner-connection.test.ts tests/ui/sidebar-layout.test.ts` passed 56 tests, TypeScript passed, changed-file lint passed, and the web interface built. The targeted Playwright journey `automatically unlocks the current server with its saved password after reload` passed against two temporary real runners after clearing the browser cookie and reloading. After the production restart, the public domain and local build both referenced `main-DWX2wW4Q.js`, and their SHA-256 hashes matched exactly (`c08dcaf7094335ae85afa8956be76af74d851928f88b978a699b2b4f39f5a857`).\n**Prevention:** Treat Connect as an explicit authentication attempt, and treat reload as a separate return journey that must restore server-authoritative authentication from saved credentials. Decide whether to authenticate from connection and credential state plus the user's action, never from a comparison of secret text. Regression coverage must test every authentication entry point, assert that the password reaches a real login path, clear the server session, revisit the app, and verify that startup restores it without manual UI actions. For live interface changes, rebuild and restart the production runner, then compare the public asset name and hash to the local build before reporting the fix as live.\n**Skill/Doc Updates:** No general skill update was needed because the existing client/server state guidance already says persisted client data cannot stand in for server-authoritative state. Try again.” message.\n+**Root Cause:** The interface build test wrote directly to `dist/interface`, replacing the hashed JavaScript assets while the production runner still held the previous `index.html` in memory. That made the old asset URL return 404 for a fresh PWA. After the runner restart exposed the current build, a separate cold-start race remained: the same-origin Connect handler required `RunnerConnection` to have already attached its runtime. The login request could succeed while that attachment was still in progress, after which the handler threw the generic client error.\n+**Fix:** Vite build tests now use unique operating-system temporary output directories through `OMNIHARNESS_INTERFACE_OUT_DIR`, so the test suite cannot modify live assets. Same-origin password authentication now belongs to `RunnerConnection`; it creates or reuses the runtime, checks the connection generation and base URL before and after login, and then reconnects. The React control no longer reaches into a partially initialized runtime.\n+**Verification:** The cold-start regression was observed failing before the manager method existed and then passed with the fix. The focused connection and UI suites passed 57 tests. The isolated Vite suite passed all 3 tests while pre/post hashes proved `dist/interface` remained unchanged. TypeScript and changed-file lint passed. The rebuilt production runner served `/assets/main-B3g8TT-T.js` through Cloudflare with HTTP 200 and the same SHA-256 hash as the local asset; public auth-session and bootstrap endpoints returned 200. A fresh Android-sized headless Chromium context logged in through the public tunnel and reached the authenticated app without a page error, then logged out cleanly.\n+**Prevention:** A test must never build into a directory served by a long-running process. Authentication transitions must be owned by the connection manager and tolerate cold initialization; components should not require an asynchronously attached runtime as a precondition for the user’s explicit Connect action.\n*** End Patch";
text(await tools.apply_patch(patch));

It wasn’t Cloudflare or your password. The server logged a successful Android login at 14:14:39, but the frontend hit a cold-start race and threw the generic error before its connection finished initializing.

I fixed and deployed both problems:

- Login now waits safely for the connection runtime.
- Build tests can no longer overwrite files used by the live server—the cause of the earlier blank screen.

Verified through the public tunnel with a fresh Android-sized browser: login succeeded and the app loaded. All 60 focused tests, TypeScript, lint, and production build passed.

Fully swipe the PWA away, reopen it, and connect again. You shouldn’t need to clear its data.

<!-- codex-event:{"kind":"progress","timestamp":"2026-08-03T12:45:47.688Z","phase":"commentary"} -->
## Codex progress · 2026-08-03T12:45:47.688Z

I found a specific race that fits the phone’s records: while you’re entering the password, the offline connection keeps scheduling automatic retries. If one retry starts during the successful login request, the app discards that successful login as “old” and never performs the authenticated reconnect. I’m reproducing that timing in a test before changing it.

<!-- /codex-event -->

When client state, server state, cache state, stream state, and persisted state all exist, every plan needs explicit invariants.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nNo UI surface may treat data as authoritative unless the payload proves ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and terminal state.\n\nIf those words are missing from the plan, the plan is probably baking in a race condition.\n\n## Planning Checklist\n\nFor every React app that reads server/runtime state, the plan must answer:\n\n1. **Owner:** What owns this state: server, client manager, URL, cache, stream, local storage, or worker/runtime?\n2. **Token:** What owner token protects async results: `requestId`, `runId`, `projectPath`, `operationId`, `workerId + seq`, or equivalent?\n3. **Provenance:** Is data server-authoritative, optimistic, cached preview, partial update, or historical fallback?\n4. **Completeness:** Does the payload declare what scope it is complete for? What may it erase?\n5. **Ordering:** What stable order is used: monotonic seq, `(createdAt, id)`, version, or cursor?\n6. **State machine:** What are the legal states, terminal states, and transitions?\n7. **Events:** Which server decisions are named events rather than client-side derivations?\n8. **Loading shape:** Which states are bootstrap, first load, incremental refresh, reconnect, resync, recovery, and terminal error?\n9. **Fallbacks:** Which legacy/fallback rows can render, and only after what authority is loaded?\n10. **Tests:** Which race, stale-response, event-sequence, reconnect, and merge tests prove the invariants?\n\n## Invariants To Require\n\n- Cached and optimistic data may pre-render, but cannot satisfy full-load gates.\n- Partial snapshots may add or refine state, but may not erase optimistic objects, delivered user input, read markers, or stream entries unless they declare complete scope.\n- Every async response checks that its owner token still matches before mutating visible state.\n- Mutation success handlers may navigate or clear UI only if they still own the current context, unless the action explicitly creates a new selected context.\n- Timers and polling callbacks re-check ownership immediately before acting.\n- Server decisions are emitted as named events; the client does not infer decisions by diffing snapshots.\n- SSE/WebSocket streams have event ids, replay/resume, and an explicit resync path.\n- Loading booleans are split by lifecycle stage. A leaf stream refresh must not unmount the whole page.\n- Append-only content has one writer, one reader, stable ids, and monotonic cursors.\n- Fallback DB rows or historical rows are gated behind stream loading and deduped by stable id plus safe equivalence.\n- Status classifiers distinguish active, runnable, blocked, awaiting user, terminal, stale, and recoverable states.\n- \"Latest\" queries have deterministic tie-breakers. Timestamp-only ordering is not enough.\n- Hot paths use bounded reads and do not synchronously load large bodies, bridge probes, schema setup, or heavy app graphs.\n- Process-local caches have explicit TTL/size bounds and invalidation rules.\n\n## Test Matrix\n\nPick the rows that match the work. Do not rely on one happy-path UI test.\n\n| Risk | Test shape |\n| --- | --- |\n| Stale async response | Start request A, switch owner, resolve A, assert it cannot mutate B |\n| Optimistic object erased | Create local optimistic state, apply stale/partial snapshot, assert object remains |\n| Cache masquerades as loaded | Hydrate cache preview, assert full-load gate waits for server authority |\n| Mutation steals navigation | Start mutation, switch selection, resolve mutation, assert focus stays put |\n| Timer/poll stale-fire | Use fake timers or deferred promises; callback must re-check owner before acting |\n| Snapshot merge erases stream | Apply partial snapshot missing known entries, assert entries/read markers remain |\n| Event stream gap | Bootstrap snapshot, emit events during disconnect, reconnect with last id, assert replay or resync |\n| Server decision invisible | Exercise branch and assert named event such as `blocked`, `refused`, `gave_up`, or `error.surfaced` |\n| State classifier wrong | Table-test every status into active/runnable/terminal/recoverable buckets |\n| Fallback duplicates stream | Load fallback rows then stream entries, assert no duplicate or false chronology |\n| Hot path bloats | Assert snapshots carry cursors not bodies; route returns before DB/heavy imports when possible |\n| Timestamp tie | Insert equal timestamps, assert deterministic order by id/seq |\n\nUse headless HTTP/SSE tests for control-plane decisions. Use React/unit tests for manager merging and ownership guards. recovery;\n- cache or optimistic data treated as authoritative without provenance;\n- async callbacks that mutate state without checking owner tokens;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- custom layout as the first implementation path when a relevant ShadCN Block exists.\n- Before adding any individual control, check whether `shadcn/ui` already provides a suitable control. Components must subscribe to the smallest slice they need, preferably with selector hooks and equality checks, so unrelated UI does not re-render.\n- Never let app shells, page roots, sidebars, timelines, or other broad containers subscribe to an entire high-churn Manager snapshot when they only need stable fields. Do not put an entire page, app shell, sidebar, timeline, composer, settings surface, and data boot path behind one giant client component unless there is a deliberate reason.\n- SSR is only useful if the initial HTML contains meaningful above-the-fold UI or data. If `curl` for the route only shows a boot shell, script payloads, or empty placeholders, the route is not meaningfully server-rendered even if SSR is technically enabled.\n- Server-render the first useful screen by fetching route-stable bootstrap data on the server: auth/session state, settings needed to choose the shell, selected route ids, and initial page/snapshot data. Hydrate Managers or query caches from that bootstrap data; do not wait for client `useEffect()` plus client fetches before the first meaningful paint.\n- Use client effects for browser-only concerns: localStorage-only preferences, notifications, SSE/WebSocket subscriptions, focus management, and post-paint refreshes. Do not use effects as the only path for data required to decide what the initial screen is.\n- In Next dev, first request time includes compilation. Distinguish cold compile cost from runtime slowness before optimizing the wrong layer.\n\n## Import And Bundle Hygiene\n\n- Keep imports proportional to the UI being rendered. Do not import an entire complex surface for a tiny control; split shared tiny controls into their own files instead of importing them from heavy feature modules.\n- Lazy-load rarely opened or route-conditional surfaces with dynamic imports: settings dialogs, side panels, file viewers, terminals, worker inspectors, onboarding flows, QR/pairing dialogs, and large markdown/code viewers.\n- Avoid package and barrel imports that drag in whole icon packs, design systems, syntax highlighters, markdown stacks, charting libraries, or component suites for one glyph or one primitive. Do not import a popover/dialog/menu stack for a low-value dropdown unless search, virtualization, or rich item rendering is genuinely needed.\n- Use subpath imports when a package supports them. If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information\n   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**\n   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion\n\n5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**\n\n   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**\n   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place\n   - Fixes require \"massive refactoring\" to implement\n   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere\n\n   **STOP and question fundamentals:**\n   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?\n   - Are we \"sticking with it through sheer inertia\"?\n   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?\n\n   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**\n\n   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.\n\n## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process\n\nIf you catch yourself thinking:\n- \"Quick fix for now, investigate later\"\n- \"Just try changing X and see if it works\"\n- \"Add multiple changes, run tests\"\n- \"Skip the test, I'll manually verify\"\n- \"It's probably X, let me fix that\"\n- \"I don't fully understand but this might work\"\n- \"Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently\"\n- \"Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]\"\n- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow\n- **\"One more fix attempt\" (when already tried 2+)**\n- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**\n\n**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**\n\n**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)\n\n## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong\n\n**Watch for these redirections:**\n- \"Is that not happening?\" - You assumed without verifying\n- \"Will it show us...?\" - You should have added evidence gathering\n- \"Stop guessing\" - You're proposing fixes without understanding\n- \"Ultrathink this\" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms\n- \"We're stuck?\" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working\n\n**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.\n\n## Common Rationalizations\n\n| Excuse | Reality |\n|--------|---------|\n| \"Issue is simple, don't need process\" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |\n| \"Emergency, no time for process\" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |\n| \"Just try this first, then investigate\" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |\n| \"I'll write test after confirming fix works\" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |\n| \"Multiple fixes at once saves time\" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |\n| \"Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern\" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |\n| \"I see the problem, let me fix it\" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |\n| \"One more fix attempt\" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |\n\n## Quick Reference\n\n| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |\n|-------|---------------|------------------|\n| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |\n| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |\n| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |\n| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |\n\n## When Process Reveals \"No Root Cause\"\n\nIf systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:\n\n1. You've completed the process\n2. Document what you investigated\n3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)\n4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation\n\n**But:** 95% of \"no root cause\" cases are incomplete investigation.\n\n## Supporting Techniques\n\nThese techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:\n\n- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger\n- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause\n- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling\n\n**Related skills:**\n- **ultrapowers:test-driven-development** - For creating failing test case (Phase 4, Step 1)\n- **ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs** - Record reusable lessons from meaningful architecture, storage, memory, persistence, control-plane, and system-level bugs\n- **ultrapowers:verification-before-completion** - Verify fix worked before claiming success\n\n## Real-World Impact\n\nFrom debugging sessions:\n- Systematic approach: 15-30 minutes to fix\n- Random fixes approach: 2-3 hours of thrashing\n- First-time fix rate: 95% vs 40%\n- New bugs introduced: Near zero vs common\n---\nname: instrumenting-control-planes\ndescription: Use when building, planning, reviewing, or debugging apps with backend decisions, agent workflows, long-running jobs, SSE/WebSocket streams, recovery paths, deletes, retries, or user-visible failures\n---\n\n# Instrumenting Control Planes\n\nBuild the control plane as a product surface. If the server decides, refuses, retries, spawns, deletes, recovers, gives up, or fails, that decision must be observable by users, operators, and tests.\n\nIf a React UI consumes the control plane through server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, or persisted runtime state, also use `client-server-state-invariants`.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nEvery meaningful server-side state transition emits a named, durable event. The UI and tests consume the same production event surface.\n\nDo not rely on snapshot diffs, rendered DOM state, logs only, or client-side re-derivation to prove what the server decided.\n\n## Hot Path Rule\n\nNo user bootstrap, catalog, status, reconnect, or recovery request may depend on a lock-prone database write path or external health probe finishing. Serve these paths from a bounded read model, memory cache, append-only event log, or stale-but-marked snapshot; queue reconciliation writes outside the request. Every dependency on a database or bridge call in a hot path needs a short timeout, cancellation, and an explicit degraded response.\n\nIf SQLite, local files, or a single-writer store is used, assume writer contention can freeze readers at the worst moment. Use one writer, WAL/busy-timeout discipline, short transactions, bounded queues, and headless chaos tests that run bootstrap/reload while writes are active. A 25s UI request is a control-plane failure, even if the database eventually returns.\n\n## Event Contract\n\nFor each backend or agent workflow, define:\n\n- named events for decisions: `worker.spawned`, `worker.reattached`, `plan.ready`, `plan.review.blocked`, `recovery.gave_up`, `conversation.delete_failed`;\n- payloads with stable ids, `prev`/`next` status when relevant, reason codes, and enough context to debug;\n- `error.surfaced` or an equivalent user-facing failure event for every failure the user should know about;\n- durable persistence or a bounded replay buffer so short disconnects do not erase history;\n- a scriptable read path: CLI, HTTP endpoint, sqlite query, or event log command.\n\nIf a decision cannot be asserted from this surface, the design is incomplete.\n\nIf debugging a control-plane failure reveals a reusable lesson, use `ultrapowers:learning-from-bugs` after the fix is verified.\n\n## Streaming Requirements\n\nFor SSE or WebSocket-like streams:\n\n- emit named events alongside any snapshot/update frame;\n- include monotonic event ids;\n- support resume from the last seen id;\n- replay missed events from a bounded buffer;\n- emit an explicit resync-required event when replay is impossible;\n- bootstrap from a snapshot, then tail events.\n\nSnapshots show current truth. Named events show why it became true.\n\n## Testing Standard\n\nControl-plane tests should usually be headless HTTP/SSE scenario tests, not browser tests. Browser automation is for UI behavior; control-plane tests assert server decisions directly.\n\nWrite scenario assertions as event transcripts:\n\n```ts\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.spawned\", { runId });\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.status\", { next: \"running\" });\nchaos.killServer();\nchaos.restartServer();\nexpect(events).toHaveEmitted(\"worker.reattached\", { runId });\nexpect(events).not.toHaveEmitted(\"worker.recreated\", { runId });\n```\n\nChaos belongs outside production code paths: drop connections in the client, fail fetches in the harness, restart the server process, and use seeds for reproducibility.\n\n## Refuse These Shapes\n\n- silent early returns in server methods;\n- swallowed `catch` blocks;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- response-code-only user failures;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- tests that infer control-plane behavior from rendered state;\n- delete handlers that do not enumerate dependent rows or emit typed failure events;\n- recovery loops without terminal events such as `gave_up` or `abandoned`;\n- request handlers that wait on inline reconciliation writes, SQLite contention, or bridge `/doctor` checks before returning bootstrap data;\n- test-only behavior branches in production code.\n\n## Design Checklist\n\nBefore implementing a backend or agent workflow, answer:\n\n1. What decisions can this workflow make?\n2. What named event is emitted for each decision, including refusal and failure?\n3. Where are events persisted or buffered?\n4. How does a client resume after disconnect?\n5. Which request paths must keep working while persistence or bridge dependencies are slow, locked, or stale?\n6. How can a CLI or test harness inspect the exact event sequence without the UI?\n7. Which headless scenario proves the happy path, failure path, recovery path, terminal state, and hot-path timeout/degraded path?\n8. Which client state consumes these events, and how does it prove ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and replay/resync?\n\nIf the answer is \"the UI can figure it out\", name the missing event instead.\n---\nname: client-server-state-invariants\ndescription: Use when planning, building, reviewing, or debugging React apps with server state, optimistic UI, caches, polling, SSE/WebSocket streams, background jobs, persistence, or client/server synchronization\n---\n\n# Client Server State Invariants\n\nReact bugs often expose deeper ownership mistakes. When client state, server state, cache state, stream state, and persisted state all exist, every plan needs explicit invariants.\n\n## Core Rule\n\nNo UI surface may treat data as authoritative unless the payload proves ownership, freshness, completeness, ordering, and terminal state.\n\nIf those words are missing from the plan, the plan is probably baking in a race condition.\n\n## Planning Checklist\n\nFor every React app that reads server/runtime state, the plan must answer:\n\n1. **Owner:** What owns this state: server, client manager, URL, cache, stream, local storage, or worker/runtime?\n2. **Token:** What owner token protects async results: `requestId`, `runId`, `projectPath`, `operationId`, `workerId + seq`, or equivalent?\n3. **Provenance:** Is data server-authoritative, optimistic, cached preview, partial update, or historical fallback?\n4. **Completeness:** Does the payload declare what scope it is complete for? What may it erase?\n5. **Ordering:** What stable order is used: monotonic seq, `(createdAt, id)`, version, or cursor?\n6. **State machine:** What are the legal states, terminal states, and transitions?\n7. **Events:** Which server decisions are named events rather than client-side derivations?\n8. **Loading shape:** Which states are bootstrap, first load, incremental refresh, reconnect, resync, recovery, and terminal error?\n9. **Fallbacks:** Which legacy/fallback rows can render, and only after what authority is loaded?\n10. **Tests:** Which race, stale-response, event-sequence, reconnect, and merge tests prove the invariants?\n\n## Invariants To Require\n\n- Cached and optimistic data may pre-render, but cannot satisfy full-load gates.\n- Partial snapshots may add or refine state, but may not erase optimistic objects, delivered user input, read markers, or stream entries unless they declare complete scope.\n- Every async response checks that its owner token still matches before mutating visible state.\n- Mutation success handlers may navigate or clear UI only if they still own the current context, unless the action explicitly creates a new selected context.\n- Timers and polling callbacks re-check ownership immediately before acting.\n- Server decisions are emitted as named events; the client does not infer decisions by diffing snapshots.\n- SSE/WebSocket streams have event ids, replay/resume, and an explicit resync path.\n- Loading booleans are split by lifecycle stage. A leaf stream refresh must not unmount the whole page.\n- Append-only content has one writer, one reader, stable ids, and monotonic cursors.\n- Fallback DB rows or historical rows are gated behind stream loading and deduped by stable id plus safe equivalence.\n- Status classifiers distinguish active, runnable, blocked, awaiting user, terminal, stale, and recoverable states.\n- \"Latest\" queries have deterministic tie-breakers. Timestamp-only ordering is not enough.\n- Hot paths use bounded reads and do not synchronously load large bodies, bridge probes, schema setup, or heavy app graphs.\n- Process-local caches have explicit TTL/size bounds and invalidation rules.\n\n## Test Matrix\n\nPick the rows that match the work. Do not rely on one happy-path UI test.\n\n| Risk | Test shape |\n| --- | --- |\n| Stale async response | Start request A, switch owner, resolve A, assert it cannot mutate B |\n| Optimistic object erased | Create local optimistic state, apply stale/partial snapshot, assert object remains |\n| Cache masquerades as loaded | Hydrate cache preview, assert full-load gate waits for server authority |\n| Mutation steals navigation | Start mutation, switch selection, resolve mutation, assert focus stays put |\n| Timer/poll stale-fire | Use fake timers or deferred promises; callback must re-check owner before acting |\n| Snapshot merge erases stream | Apply partial snapshot missing known entries, assert entries/read markers remain |\n| Event stream gap | Bootstrap snapshot, emit events during disconnect, reconnect with last id, assert replay or resync |\n| Server decision invisible | Exercise branch and assert named event such as `blocked`, `refused`, `gave_up`, or `error.surfaced` |\n| State classifier wrong | Table-test every status into active/runnable/terminal/recoverable buckets |\n| Fallback duplicates stream | Load fallback rows then stream entries, assert no duplicate or false chronology |\n| Hot path bloats | Assert snapshots carry cursors not bodies; route returns before DB/heavy imports when possible |\n| Timestamp tie | Insert equal timestamps, assert deterministic order by id/seq |\n\nUse headless HTTP/SSE tests for control-plane decisions. Use React/unit tests for manager merging and ownership guards. Use Playwright only for real UI layout, focus, scroll, mobile computed styles, and visible affordances.\n\n## Refuse These Shapes\n\n- one `isLoading` boolean for bootstrap, refresh, reconnect, and recovery;\n- cache or optimistic data treated as authoritative without provenance;\n- async callbacks that mutate state without checking owner tokens;\n- client-side derivation of server decisions;\n- snapshot diffs used as the only way to know what happened;\n- event streams without ids or resume;\n- timestamp-only \"latest\" queries;\n- parallel transcript or persistence surfaces that the frontend must reconcile;\n- unbounded process caches introduced to hide slow storage;\n- tests that prove only the DOM result when the bug is a server decision.\n\n## Review Prompt\n\nAsk this before implementation starts:\n\n> What can arrive late, out of order, partially, twice, or after the user changes context, and what test proves it cannot corrupt visible state?\n"
  }
